name: Specialization of knowledge and activity
plain_explanation: In classical Athens a capable man was expected to be soldier, politician, and thinker all at once (Russell's examples: Socrates, Xenophon, Plato). In the Hellenistic world this stopped: soldiers were soldiers, mathematicians were mathematicians, administrators were administrators, and no one aspired to Aristotle's kind of universal competence.
precise_definition: The Hellenistic shift toward professional specialization in science, administration, the military, and philosophy, replacing the classical ideal of the all-round citizen-philosopher-statesman.
why_it_mattered: It explains, for Russell, why Alexandrian science (Euclid, Archimedes, Aristarchus, Apollonius) reached a technical level equal to anything earlier while philosophy after Aristotle produced no new universal system until the Neoplatonists five centuries later.
historical_origin: A consequence of Macedonian rule removing real political power from the citizen body of the old poleis, so that public life ceased to require an all-round competence.
examples: Euclid, Aristarchus, Archimedes, and Apollonius as pure mathematicians uninterested in philosophical originality
Uneducated Macedonian soldiers employing Greek experts for irrigation and drainage in Egypt
competing_positions: The earlier classical ideal, exemplified by Socrates (soldier and philosopher), Xenophon (general and writer), and Pythagorean mathematicians who sought to govern cities
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Follows directly from the loss of self-government in the Greek cities under Macedonian rule.
